en: That wise, mace-wielding elephant.
When you enter battle, he is your helmet;
When you charge against the enemy,
He is your spear, stout-shafted and sharp-tipped;
When you stoop to strike the foe,
He is your mace from Emil.
If you train him well, none like him can be found;
He is your falcon, a keen goshawk.
If you receive him, he will be your stronghold;
Be sure to take him to yourself.”
His mother Chürök began before Seytek
To raise the clamor,
And began to stir
An incurable calamity.
While Aichürök was still speaking,
Before she had finished her words,
Divinely guarded Külchoro
Prepared as though to flee.
Inspiration came to him from the unseen;
He stiffened like cured leather,
His shovel-like teeth gleaming white.
The blazing fire within him was boundless,
Its like had never been born;
He was a tempest sprung from mankind,
And no such man existed among warriors.
He pranced sideways like a racehorse,
And began to speak with laughter,
Gleaming in his mail coat.
Külchoro, fairer than any man,
From the pavilion with golden pillars
Toward his sister-in-law, a woman like the moon,
Came walking softly.
Aichürök was his sister-in-law,
Yet more than that, his mother;
She had come when he was tiny,
And he had clung to her in a mother’s stead,
For she had fed him doe’s milk.
To the sister-in-law he regarded as his mother,
Choro approached and said:
“Sister, it is truly the Jediger whom I face,
And valiant Kyyaz with whom I contend.
Your Külchoro is like hardened red iron;
Let no one say he met a true slaughter
And perished there.
I was your renowned brother-in-law,
And you were my heroic sister-in-law.
Have you a coat for me to wear?
Let me proudly don your coat;
The one I must confront is valiant Kyyaz.
I shall face him once and see;
If fate has come, I shall die.
I shall behold the unyielding truth
That the Creator has inscribed for me.
If death comes and my days are done,
Do not grieve for a servant like me.
If I should die,
I was a son worth no more than dogskin;
If I survive,
I am a servant worth no more than sheepskin.
How could I be one who girded his waist firmly,
One born of the same blood as the falcon,
Sprung from the pure loins
Of Manas, radiant as the moon?
How could I have burst forth, tearing
The womb of my poor mother Kanykey?
When was I ever a son of Manas?
If my strength fails and power leaves me,
I shall die at the hands of valiant Kyyaz;
He looks ready to strike.
He rages like a tiger,
And none who clash with him survive.
His movement is like a gathering storm,
His countenance like a snowy mountainside,
His menace like a deep abyss;
Let alone the Jediger, if he is roused,
He seems able to swallow the world.
He rages like a tiger,
And none who fight him survive.
When he opens his cavernous mouth,
The cold blast issuing from it
Is like the wind along a mountain ridge.
The broad expanse of his two cheeks
Is like a vast blue field spread wide.
Your dark-browed Külchoro
Looks ready to devour all who confront him.
His upturned mustache
Is like a saber from Bukhara.
The icy glare of his two eyes
Is like flame burning upon a highland.
The narrow bridge of his nose
Is like a saber’s sheath.
When you look into his eye sockets,
They resemble the bed of a dried-up river.
The fierce, dark-browed warrior
Looks ready to drain whoever meets him.
The heroic Choro’s imposing form
Seems able to turn a mighty river.
If his stubborn fury seizes him,
He will unleash a grievous disaster;
If he comes within reach of Kyyaz,
He will seize him and dash him to the ground.
Not valiant Kyyaz alone—
Though the Jediger swarm in countless hosts,
He will slaughter them without leaving a hair.
When the falcon stirs,
Would the whole world dare confront him?
If all creation attacked in fury,
Could any man defeat Choro?
My valiant prince was lost,
My two knees buckled,
My suffering soul was overcome,
My tiny life cried out,
My whole body quaked
When I was caught in a net
That no leap could break.
My two hands were bound,
My two eyes stared wide,
When I fell captive.
When the seething Jediger host
Closed in and reached me,
They were thousands, and I alone,
When I fell into their hands.
They stripped off my robe as plunder
And slashed my neck ten times.
They tormented me, demanding blood-price,
And took as spoil my kangadai,
My trousers that no bullet could pierce.
They showed me many marvels,
Crippled both my hands,
And stripped my robe as booty,
Making my eyes behold
Things no man should ever see.”
Thus Külchoro spoke,
And before he had closed his mouth,
Aichürök brought the blue saddlebag,
The great green-hued camel saddlebag,
A saddlebag filled with treasures,
No ordinary pack for a gelded camel—
That saddlebag held things beyond price;
Within this saddlebag,
What was there, and what was not!
Kalyipa entered and took out a letter,
She who had been branded a dark-faced shrew:
“The kangadai spoken of before
Was meant for my son and brother-in-law to wear,
So he might strike the foe without tiring,
So he might charge whenever the enemy fled.
If I fail to understand this,
I will surrender my tiny life.
If my destined death has not arrived,
Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
I shall make a spectacle of you;
I shall seize whoever attacks me
And destroy whoever assails me.
I shall hunt down whoever meets me,
And if Providence brings me face-to-face
With my adversary Kyyaz,
I shall drink his blood.
I have gathered what was scattered,
My faith is all I desire.
Brave Kyyaz is the one I shall grapple with,
The enemy on whom I have fixed my gaze.
If I cannot cross the dark ridge,
What mark of manhood is there
If I cannot wrestle and take revenge,
Cutting off heads and spilling blood,
Thrusting spears and venting fury,
Meeting face-to-face,
Firing guns and drawing bows,
And crashing together in battle?
With their fangs laid bare,
Before dead horses lie in heaps,
With their fine moustaches stroked,
Before many brave men are slain,
Can there be any glorious deed?
Can a brave man who fears slaughter
Truly be called a man?
If foes confront each other
Yet the hidden, razor-sharp Zulfiqar
Is not driven into the very heart,
Can there be valor in a hero?
In this world that lasts but two days,
Does it become a hero to fear?
Brave Kyyaz is the one I shall fight—
My sister-in-law, lovely as the moon,
Is there armor I may wear into battle?
My valiant mother Kanykey—
How many robes did she give as gifts?
Your warrior companion could bear no more,
And mountain-like Kyyaz would not be stopped;
He would come to Aichürök,
And keep humiliating her, calling her a slave,
Thinking God had delivered him a slave.
On the road by which Kyyaz would come,
His courage and lionhearted valor
Had now risen above all others.
Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
The fierce, illustrious hero,
He had gone out to intercept.
Eager to enter the struggle,
To avenge his prince,
He made his weapons ready,
And buckled on his naked sword,
Hanging the golden-cheeked battle-axe
From his bare forearm,
And praying to the spirit
Of Manas, departed to the other world.
Against Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
He went to wage a furious fight.
If his strength boiled up and proved enough,
He would drink his blood.
If his fate arrived and his days were done,
“Let me die at brave Kyyaz’s hand;
But if we clash unexpectedly,
And fortune grants me strength,
May I suck and drink
The black blood within him like kumiss.”
He swiftly invoked Baabedin,
And, honoring his father Manas’s way,
Called upon Aituyak by name.
The lion-born warrior
Swiftly uttered every prayer
And went to the road where Kyyaz would come—
To the mouth of the dark ravine,
To the ridge where the banner vanished,
To the blunt projecting spur,
To the broken Aksai pasture,
Upon the gaping mountain shoulder,
Thinking, “If the warriors meet face-to-face,
Will their bullets miss?”
Its lining was worked in silk,
Stitched by a wretched, diligent craftsman,
Layered, riveted, and sewn,
So that merely looking at it
Made a man’s eyes slide away.
Trimmed and bordered with sharpened steel,
When it was readied for gunfire,
A vast fortune had been spent.
Its weakest places were cut away,
Then filed and cast from steel,
Its edging was drawn out in gold,
And whole sable skins
Were fitted around the cuffs.
Its collar had folded ornament,
Its cuffs were reinforced
And embroidered with gold.
A musket ball could not cut it,
Nor could a rifle ball penetrate it;
It was sewn throughout with sharpened steel,
So that in close combat
A man’s hand slid off it.
Showing her care as a sister-in-law,
She dressed Külchoro in the kangadai,
The armor no bullet could pierce.
The battle garb Külchoro wore
Had not the smallest hole anywhere;
